newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: FMC's Argentine lithium mine starting up.
newsitem.headline: FMC's Argentine lithium mine starting up.

text.p: The Fenix lithium mine being developed by FMC Corp in northwestern Argentina is producing its first brine and will soon begin output of lithium carbonate, a top mine official said Monday.
"We should have the first lithium carbonate in the next few weeks," Gonzalo Tufino, general manager of FMC's local subsiary FMC Minera del Altiplano, told Reuters by telephone.

The mine began producing brine -- the first step in lithium compound production -- on schedule in December. The last of the mine's three plants is due to come onstream in late June or early July, allowing Fenix to begin producing lithium chloride.
The mine has run into some unexpected delays due to unusual summer snow blocking the Andean mountain pass to Chile, which slowed down equipment deliveries, Tufino said.
"We twice sent out the mine's own equipment to clear the pass in winter, but I didn't expect the pass to be blocked in summer," Tufino said.
Fenix will ship its lithium products from the Chilean port of Antofagasta.

The $68-million Fenix is the first of a new wave of modern mines being brought into production in Argentina, a result of free market reforms which attracted foreign minerals investors starting in the early 1990s.

The mine is being built at 13,000 feet (4,000 meters) above sea level on the Salar del Hombre Muerto salt lake straddling the provinces of Catamarca and Salta. FMC said in 1996 that Fenix's startup would allow it to close its plant in Bessamer City, North Carolina, some time this year.
To produce 45 million pounds, lithium carbonate equivalent, a year, Fenix will provide the first major lithium production outside Chile or the United States.

It will enter a long cozy lithium market now frazzled by the aggressive marketing of Chilean newcomers Sociedad Quimica y Minera de Chile (Soquimich), which started producing at its Minsal mine last October.

The largest consumers of lithium carbonate, a fine white powder, are the glass, ceramics and primary aluminum industries. Demand is also strong from U.S. smelters where lithium is used for improving energy efficiency. It is used, in smaller quantities, as a treatement for manic depression.
